Credit: Caleb Kenna for ProPublica Posted in Pollution Vermont Was Supposed to Get an Audit of Its Lake Champlain Cleanup. It Never Happened. Halfway through a 20-year push to get Vermont’s waterways in line with tougher EPA standards, some lawmakers worry the project’s strategies aren’t as cost-effective as they could be — especially as a state-mandated audit was never done. by Circle of Blue November 16, 2026 November 16, 2026 Share this article: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky By Jonathan Mingle , Seven Days This story was originally published by ProPublica . This article was produced for ProPublica’s Local Reporting Network in partnership with Seven Days . Sign up for Dispatches to get our stories in your inbox every week. This summer, Vermont’s Clean Water Board celebrated a milestone: Over the past decade, the state has invested nearly a billion dollars to clean up its polluted streams, rivers and lakes. The vast majority of that money has gone toward Lake Champlain. “I think that’s something to be extremely proud of,” said Douglas Farnham, the board’s chair. Sign up Vermont was supposed to get an independent evaluation of what it has gotten for all that money. But that study was never done. A decade ago, Vermont lawmakers mandated that the board submit an audit from an outside environmental consultant to determine whether the projects the state had invested in to improve water quality were working. The audit also was meant to examine whether the state’s agriculture and natural resource agencies are doing enough to enforce water quality regulations on farms, which are the biggest source of phosphorus in Lake Champlain. Lake Champlain has been overloaded with phosphorus-laden runoff from farms, roads and urban sewers for decades. That pollution fuels potentially toxic blue-green algae blooms that have raised health concerns and hurt the state’s tourism industry. Under sustained pressure from citizens, environmental advocates and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Vermont’s leaders embarked on an ambitious initiative to improve the lake’s water quality, enshrined in the state’s landmark 2015 Clean Water Act.
